hero.title: Health Beyond Hurdles / Santé Sans Obstacles
hero.subtitle: Dedicated to improving access to health information, non-clinical healthcare services, and community support for newcomers and underserved communities in Saskatchewan.

overview.title: Who we are
paragraphs: We are a proposed bilingual nonprofit based in Regina, created to close a specific gap: newcomers arrive in Saskatchewan with the right to healthcare, but not the map to reach it.

Our work is non-clinical. We do not diagnose, treat, or replace healthcare professionals. We explain how the system works in plain language, and connect people to the services, organizations, and professionals already equipped to help them.
The Newcomer Health Navigation Project is our first program, piloting in Regina before expanding across the province.

mission.title: Mission
mission.body: To help newcomers in Canada and underserved communities navigate and understand Saskatchewan's healthcare system by providing them with the support, education, and resources they need to make informed decisions about their health and well-being.

vision.title: Vision
vision.body: A Saskatchewan where every person, regardless of language, culture, income, or immigration experience, can confidently access healthcare services, understand their options, and participate actively in decisions concerning their health.

challenge.title: What stands in the way
challenge.subtitle: Newcomers often arrive with little knowledge of how Saskatchewan's healthcare system operates. A combination of everyday barriers can turn a routine health need into a crisis.

items.title: Language barriers
items.body: Conversational English or French isn't the same as understanding medical terminology, consent forms, or instructions given during a stressful appointment.

items.title: Unfamiliar terminology
items.body: Referrals, requisitions, deductibles, HealthLine: the vocabulary of the system is rarely explained in plain language.

items.title: Cultural differences
items.body: Expectations around appointments, consent, and provider relationships can differ significantly from a person's home country.

items.title: Transportation challenges
items.body: Getting to a clinic, pharmacy, or appointment isn't always straightforward without a vehicle or transit knowledge.

items.title: Limited service knowledge
items.body: Many newcomers simply don't know what services exist, who provides them, or when to use which one.

challenge.consequence: Together, these barriers can prevent people from seeking care, delay treatment, or push them toward the emergency department when another option would have served them better.

bilingualism.title: Bilingualism is who we are, not a feature we added
paragraphs: We understand the hardship of facing a health system in a language you are still learning. Conversational English is not the same as understanding a consent form, a prescription label, or instructions given in a stressful moment.

So we work in both languages from the start. Every guide, workshop, intake conversation, and public communication exists in French and in English, with the same care given to each. Neither is a last-minute translation of the other.

We use plain language instead of medical jargon, and we explain key healthcare terms in both languages. When someone needs a language we do not work in, we connect them to interpretation services rather than leave them to manage alone.
commitments: Equal quality and depth in French and English, never an afterthought
Plain language instead of medical terminology, with key terms explained in both
Bilingual volunteers, advisors, board members, and partners
Direct connections to Francophone organizations and interpretation services

longTerm.title: Where we go from here
longTerm.body: Growth follows evidence, not ambition. Each phase has to work before the next one begins.

phases.label: Phase 1
phases.title: Regina pilot
phases.body: Publish the bilingual newcomer healthcare guide, build partnerships with settlement agencies, and train the first cohort of bilingual volunteers.

phases.label: Phase 2
phases.title: Measure and refine
phases.body: Track participants served, languages requested, referrals completed, and changes in confidence navigating the system. Revise the guides around what people actually ask.

phases.label: Phase 3
phases.title: Saskatchewan-wide
phases.body: Extend distribution to Saskatoon, Prince Albert, Moose Jaw, and rural communities through partner locations, adding topic-specific resources as needs emerge.

phases.label: Phase 4
phases.title: Beyond navigation
phases.body: Add community health workshops, maternal-health education for newcomers, senior health navigation, and youth health education.

longTerm.closing: Through community partnerships, trained volunteers, and culturally respectful education, we work to ensure that newcomers are not left to navigate Saskatchewan's healthcare system alone.

hero.title: The Newcomer Health Navigation Project
hero.subtitle: A bilingual health education and navigation initiative for newcomers who have lived in Saskatchewan for less than five years and currently reside in Saskatchewan.

overview.title: How the program works
paragraphs: The program will primarily operate by creating bilingual educational resources in French and English, available as downloadable PDF guides and printed booklets, distributed throughout the community in locations newcomers already visit: newcomer and settlement agencies, community centres, libraries, schools, post-secondary institutions, places of worship, and other community partner locations.

Guides use simple language, clear explanations, visual elements, and step-by-step instructions, with French and English content given equal importance. Resources provide general, non-clinical information only: they do not diagnose conditions, recommend treatments, interpret test results, or replace advice from licensed healthcare professionals. All health-related content will be reviewed by qualified healthcare professionals before publication whenever possible.

The first major resource will be a bilingual newcomer healthcare guide: a general introduction to the provincial healthcare system that directs readers to trusted organizations and service providers for individualized assistance. The PDF will be shared electronically through partner organizations, social media, email newsletters, community websites, and QR codes in public locations; printed copies will be distributed at newcomer events, orientation sessions, workshops, health fairs, and community gatherings.

The program's role is to provide education and orientation, not individualized medical advice. Readers are always encouraged to contact an appropriate healthcare professional, HealthLine 811, emergency services, or a trusted community organization for assistance specific to their personal situation.

topics.title: What the guides cover
topics.intro: The bilingual guides and booklets may cover topics such as:
items: How Saskatchewan's healthcare system works
How to apply for, renew, or update a Saskatchewan health card
Differences between family doctors, nurse practitioners, pharmacists, public health nurses, specialists, walk-in clinics, urgent care centres, and emergency departments
Where to go for different types of healthcare needs
How to find healthcare and community services in Saskatchewan
How to book, prepare for, and attend a healthcare appointment
How medical referrals, laboratory testing, diagnostic imaging, and prescriptions generally work
When to contact HealthLine 811, call 911, visit an emergency department, or speak with another healthcare provider
Questions newcomers may want to ask during a healthcare appointment
Common healthcare and medical terminology in both French and English
How to access mental health, dental, reproductive health, maternal health, public health, vaccination, and pharmacy services
How to locate services offered in French or English
Patient rights, informed consent, privacy, and confidentiality
How to access interpretation or language-support services
How to connect with settlement agencies, transportation assistance, food programs, housing supports, and other resources affecting health and well-being
A list of trusted provincial and community healthcare resources
Shorter fact sheets, checklists, posters, infographics, appointment-preparation worksheets, healthcare vocabulary lists, and emergency-information cards

education.title: Bilingual health education
education.intro: Education is a core part of the program. We will develop practical French and English resources on topics such as:
items: How to access healthcare in Saskatchewan
The difference between primary, urgent, and emergency care
How to prepare for a medical appointment
How pharmacy services work
How to understand prescriptions and medication instructions
Preventive healthcare and routine screening
Mental health and community support services
Patient rights, consent, privacy, and confidentiality
Maternal, child, and family health services
Health services for seniors and people living with disabilities
How to communicate health concerns clearly and confidently
education.note: Educational workshops will be designed in collaboration with healthcare professionals and community organizations, and reviewed regularly to remain accurate, current, and appropriate for Saskatchewan residents.

quality.title: How we keep information accurate
items: Consult newcomers about the questions and challenges they experience
Work with healthcare professionals to review health-related information
Collaborate with settlement workers and community organizations
Use reliable Saskatchewan and Canadian healthcare sources
Include the date of publication or last update on each resource
Review links, phone numbers, addresses, and eligibility requirements regularly
Collect feedback from readers and partner organizations, and update or reprint guides as information changes

distribution.title: Where you'll find the guides
distribution.body: The PDF version will be available online and shared electronically through partner organizations, social media, email newsletters, community websites, and QR codes displayed in public locations. Printed copies will be placed in accessible community spaces and distributed during newcomer events, orientation sessions, workshops, health fairs, and community gatherings.
channels: Newcomer events, orientation sessions & health fairs

evaluation.title: How we'll evaluate the pilot
evaluation.body: We will track and evaluate the pilot through:
metrics: Change in participants' confidence navigating the healthcare system

whoWeServe.pilotBody: The pilot will initially focus on newcomers living in Regina and surrounding communities. hero.title: This program is only possible with bilingual volunteers
hero.subtitle: We are recruiting and training bilingual volunteers to deliver healthcare-system navigation with confidentiality, professional boundaries, cultural humility, and trauma-informed, respectful communication across languages and cultures.

items.title: Healthcare professionals
items.body: Nurses, pharmacists, physicians, and allied health professionals: your clinical knowledge helps us explain the system accurately and in plain language.

items.title: Healthcare students
items.body: Medical, nursing, pharmacy, public health, and allied health students bring valuable, current knowledge.

items.title: Retired healthcare professionals
items.body: Your years of experience are exactly what newcomers need to understand a new system with confidence.

items.title: Settlement workers
items.body: Your knowledge of the newcomer journey helps connect healthcare navigation to the bigger picture.

items.title: Experienced newcomers
items.body: Having navigated the system yourself, you can guide others with empathy and firsthand insight.

items.title: Translators & interpreters
items.body: Help ensure information is accurate, natural, and culturally appropriate in both languages.

items.title: Educators
items.body: Support the design and delivery of clear, accessible bilingual educational materials and workshops.

items.title: Community members
items.body: No specific background required, just a commitment to bilingual, respectful, judgment-free support.

training.title: Volunteer training
training.body: Every volunteer receives training before supporting participants, covering:
items: Healthcare-system navigation
Confidentiality
Professional boundaries
Cultural humility
Trauma-informed communication
Referral procedures
Emergency escalation
Respectful communication across languages and cultures

pathways.title: More ways to contribute
pathways.advisorBody: Healthcare professionals may volunteer as advisors or content reviewers, helping ensure educational information is accurate and that program activities remain within appropriate non-clinical boundaries.
pathways.peerBody: Former program participants may eventually be invited to become peer navigators, volunteers, advisors, or community ambassadors, their lived experience helping the organization remain responsive to the actual needs of newcomers.

cta.title: Ready to volunteer?
cta.body: Tell us about your background and how you'd like to help, in French, English, or both.

hero.title: Built through collaboration, not duplication
hero.subtitle: The success of this program depends on working with organizations already serving newcomers and Saskatchewan communities, not competing with them.
